{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-vt-class-std","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"76d19bd0eff338b8bb1da07a6f04671c9075067bbd038393fa285679473ef98e","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-vt-class-std:lineage:23","source_registry_sha256":"0441bafe0dc257fd56d6bd0cd9054ad2b95889f94f5d3e5e6f98fb890bf902c4","source_liveness_sha256":"13f90fd88bb623234ea3628f2ee40ced3511148c14c82097743066ee414dd040"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Road signs, highway markings and work zones","heading":"C — Road signs, highway markings and work zones","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Road signs, highway markings and work zones (part one)

FACT_ID: sec06-F01 | anchor: A01
Crossbuck signs stand at every railroad crossing to show where the tracks are, and a driver should slow down, look both ways and listen for trains before crossing [A01].
Why it matters: The crossbuck marks the tracks themselves, not just an approach.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec06-F02 | anchor: A01
A smaller sign below the crossbuck tells how many tracks the crossing has, and where there are two or more tracks one passing train can hide a second train coming the other way; gates and flashing lights may also be present [A01].
Why it matters: Multiple tracks create the hidden second train hazard.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec06-F03 | anchor: A01
A triangle shaped sign with its points cut off is displayed on vehicles that travel at slow speeds, such as farm vehicles [A01].
Why it matters: The slow moving vehicle emblem is a shape question.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec06-F04 | anchor: A01
Warning signs are placed where danger exists at all times and tell a driver to slow down; they are usually diamond shaped and yellow or green and may warn of sharp curves, unsafe intersections or dips in the road [A01].
Why it matters: Diamond and yellow means warning.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec06-F05 | anchor: A01
Some warning signs add information such as a safe speed or a distance, and a downward arrow under a school or pedestrian sign marks a crosswalk or crossing area [A01].
Why it matters: The downward arrow pinpoints the crossing.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec06-F06 | anchor: A02
Regulatory signs are rectangular with white backgrounds and state what a driver must or must not do, including speed limits, turning and passing laws and other directions [A02].
Why it matters: White rectangle means a rule you must obey.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec06-F07 | anchor: A02
Highway markings help a driver position the vehicle, direct the driver through situations, show when passing is allowed and warn of conditions ahead, and major highways carry yellow center lines [A02].
Why it matters: Yellow center lines are the baseline of all markings.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec06-F08 | anchor: A02
Center lines divide a highway into travel lanes, a multilane highway without a median uses double solid lines to separate the two opposing directions, and a broken white line divides lanes carrying traffic in the same direction [A02].
Why it matters: Yellow separates directions, white separates same direction lanes.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec06-F09 | anchor: A02
Where there is a solid line or two solid lines it is recommended not to pass, where a broken line is on your side next to a solid line you may pass when the road ahead is clear, and where the solid line is on your side and the broken line on the other you should not pass while the other lane's traffic may [A02].
Why it matters: The line on your side of the center governs your passing.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec06-F10 | anchor: A02
A continuous two way left turn lane is not a travel lane, because traffic in both directions may use it to turn left; a short distance before the turn signal, move the whole vehicle into the lane so traffic is not blocked, and turn when the way is clear [A02].
Why it matters: The whole vehicle goes into the center turn lane.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec06-F11 | anchor: A02
At a yield intersection a yield line, a row of white triangles pointing toward approaching cars, may be painted on the road to show where drivers should stop when they must yield to pedestrians or other vehicles [A02].
Why it matters: The painted triangles mark the yield stopping point.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec06-F12 | anchor: A02
When turning from one road onto a multilane road with a choice of lanes, a right turning driver must turn into the right lane and a left turning driver must first turn into the left lane [A02].
Why it matters: Turn into the nearest lane on your side.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec06-F13 | anchor: A02
Where two lanes turn in the same direction each turning lane must keep to its own path throughout the turn, multiple lanes may turn together only when lane use signs or pavement markings allow it, and a driver stays in the designated lane until the turn is complete [A02].
Why it matters: Side by side turning lanes must not drift.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec06-F14 | anchor: A03
Lane changes belong after a turn is finished, because changing lanes while turning is an illegal maneuver that leads to crashes [A03].
Why it matters: Changing lanes mid turn is illegal, not merely unwise.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec06-F15 | anchor: A03
A driver must follow through on the direction marked in the lane, so a driver in a straight arrow lane may not legally turn right or left at the intersection, and it is safer to drive around the block than to make a sudden lane change [A03].
Why it matters: The lane arrow is binding at the intersection.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec06-F16 | anchor: A03
A work zone is a highway area with construction, maintenance or utility work, and it may be stationary or a mobile operation moving slowly down the road, such as line striping, mowing or snow removal [A03].
Why it matters: Mobile operations count as work zones.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec06-F17 | anchor: A03
Many work zone crashes happen before the actual work area where drivers slow and merge, so drivers should merge into the correct lane as soon as it is safe, and most work zone crashes are rear end crashes from driving too fast for conditions and following too closely, with stopped traffic possibly hidden around a curve or over a hill [A03].
Why it matters: Rear end crashes before the work area are the typical pattern.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec06-F18 | anchor: A03
Work zone rules apply around the clock, not just in daylight, and drivers should slow to the posted limit and adjust further for weather, because speeds are lowered to protect both motorists and workers [A03].
Why it matters: Night and weekends are still work zones.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec06-F19 | anchor: A03
In a work zone give the road full attention, expect pedestrians, bicyclists and every other mode of travel, follow the signs, and avoid changing lanes, tailgating or other aggressive behavior [A03].
Why it matters: Lane changes inside the zone are discouraged.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec06-F20 | anchor: A03
Work zone drivers should merge as instructed as soon as it is safe, leave workers and equipment as much space as possible, keep a four second following distance, and be patient about delays or take another route [A03].
Why it matters: Four seconds applies in work zones too.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec06-F21 | anchor: A03
On dry pavement a passenger car traveling at sixty miles per hour needs two hundred forty feet to come to a complete stop, compared with seventy-five feet for the same car at thirty miles per hour [A03].
Why it matters: Doubling speed more than triples the stopping distance in this example.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec06-F22 | anchor: A03
Fines are doubled for speeding in a work zone [A03].
Why it matters: A short absolute rule worth a question.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec06-F23 | anchor: A04
Work zone signs are orange and shaped as diamonds or rectangles, and they warn of hazards ahead such as closed lanes, detours, rough pavement or flaggers [A04].
Why it matters: Orange is the work zone color.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec06-F24 | anchor: A04
Traffic often must stop in a work zone so equipment can move or because only one lane is open for both directions, flaggers guide traffic with stop and slow paddles or sometimes orange flags, and a flagger has legal authority to control traffic and must be obeyed [A04].
Why it matters: A flagger's paddle carries the force of law.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec06-F25 | anchor: A04
Cones, drums and barricades are channeling devices used to keep traffic out of hazardous roadwork areas and to guide it safely through the work zone [A04].
Why it matters: Three named channeling devices.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec06-F26 | anchor: A04
Flashing arrow panels guide drivers into the correct lane, and when no arrow is needed the panel shows caution mode, a straight line of blinking lights or blinking lights on its four corners, which tells drivers to slow down [A04].
Why it matters: Caution mode means slow, even without an arrow.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec06-F27 | anchor: A04
Work zones may use temporary pavement markings where white markers or lines separate lanes going the same way and yellow markers or lines separate opposing lanes, so yellow markings should be on your left and if they are not you are in the wrong lane [A04].
Why it matters: Yellow on the left is the self check for the right lane.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0037]

Misconceptions:
- A broken line anywhere in the center means you may pass: false, only a broken line on your own side permits passing; a solid line on your side forbids it.
- A two way left turn lane may be used to get ahead of traffic: false, it is not a travel lane and is entered only briefly, with the whole vehicle, just before a left turn.
- Work zone speed limits apply only when workers are visible: false, work zone rules apply around the clock and speeding fines there are doubled.
- A flagger's paddle is advisory: false, a flagger has legal authority to control traffic and must be obeyed.
- Changing lanes while completing a turn is acceptable if clear: false, it is illegal; change lanes only after the turn is complete.

Mnemonics:
- Yellow diamond warns, white rectangle rules, orange works: the three sign families by color and shape.
- Broken on my side, I may pass; solid on my side, I stay: the passing line rule.
- Yellow on the left or you are wrong: the lane check in temporary work zone markings.

Glossary:
- Crossbuck: the X shaped sign placed at every railroad crossing to mark where the tracks are
- Regulatory sign: a white rectangular sign stating what a driver must or must not do
- Warning sign: a yellow or green diamond shaped sign marking a permanent danger that calls for slowing down
- Two way left turn lane: a center lane shared by both directions for left turns only, never for through travel
- Yield line: a painted row of white triangles pointing at approaching traffic that marks where to stop when yielding
- Channeling devices: cones, drums and barricades that keep traffic out of work areas and guide it through a work zone
- Flashing arrow panel: a lighted sign that directs drivers into the correct lane or, in caution mode, shows a bar or four corner lights meaning slow down
